short: India's single tax on the supply of most goods and services, collected at each stage of sale and shared between the Centre and the states.
kid: When you buy a toy, a few extra coins are added to the price. Those coins go to the people who look after the country, to pay for roads, schools and hospitals.
detail: The Goods and Services Tax, launched on 1 July 2017 after the 101st Constitutional Amendment, replaced most indirect taxes such as central excise, service tax and state VAT. It is destination-based: on a sale within a state, the Centre collects CGST and the state collects SGST in equal halves; on a sale between states or an import, the Centre collects IGST and shares it later. Each business claims input tax credit for GST paid on its purchases, so tax falls only on the value it adds and the final consumer bears the full amount. Under the rules as of 2025, after the September 2025 overhaul, most items sit in 5% or 18% slabs, with 40% on certain luxury and sin goods, while crude oil, petrol, diesel, jet fuel, natural gas and alcoholic liquor stay outside GST. A common confusion is thinking businesses bear GST: it mostly passes through to buyers.
example: Say ABC Traders sells goods worth ₹10,000 to a buyer in the same state at an 18% rate. GST is ₹1,800, split as ₹900 CGST and ₹900 SGST. If ABC paid ₹1,080 of GST on its own purchases, it claims that as input tax credit and deposits only ₹720 with the government.
formula: GST payable = Output GST on sales - Input tax credit on purchases

short: The constitutional body of the Union Finance Minister and state finance ministers that recommends GST rates, exemptions and rules.
kid: Imagine the head teacher and every class monitor sitting at one table to agree on one rule for the whole school. They talk it over, vote, and then every class follows the same rule.
detail: The GST Council was created under Article 279A of the Constitution. It is chaired by the Union Finance Minister, and its members are the Union Minister of State for Finance and the finance ministers of every state and of union territories with legislatures. It recommends GST rates, exemptions, registration thresholds, compliance rules and dispute processes. Voting is weighted: the Centre holds one-third of the vote and the states together two-thirds, and a decision needs three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting, so neither side can push a change alone. Its meetings move markets because one decision can change prices across whole sectors, as when the 56th meeting in September 2025 approved a broad rate rationalisation. A common confusion: in the Mohit Minerals case (2022) the Supreme Court held that its recommendations are persuasive, not automatically binding on Parliament and state legislatures.
example: Say the Centre and 30 states are present and voting. The Centre carries 33.33 of 100 points and each state carries 66.67 / 30, about 2.22 points. With the Centre in favour, 19 states give 33.33 + 42.22 = 75.56 points, just above the 75 needed, while 18 states give only 33.33 + 40.00 = 73.33, so the Centre alone, or a bloc of 12 states, can block a decision.
formula: A proposal passes if weighted yes votes >= 75% of weighted votes cast, with the Centre's vote = 1/3 and all states together = 2/3

short: The total GST the government receives in a month or year, a widely watched signal of consumption and business activity.
kid: Every time someone buys something, a coin drops into a big jar for the town. Counting the jar each month shows whether people have been buying more or less.
detail: GST collections are the tax receipts under the Goods and Services Tax, published monthly by the government, usually early in the month. Gross collections add up CGST, SGST, IGST and any cess; net collections subtract refunds, mostly to exporters and to businesses whose input tax credit exceeds the tax on their sales. Because GST covers most consumption, year-on-year growth is read as a near-real-time gauge of demand, formalisation and compliance, alongside indicators such as PMI and auto sales. Two confusions to avoid. First, the figure released for a month mostly reflects sales made in the previous month, because returns are filed after the month ends. Second, growth can come from better compliance or rate changes rather than more spending, and rate cuts can lower collections even when volumes rise. April figures are usually seasonal highs because of March year-end sales.
example: Suppose gross GST collections for a month are ₹1.76 lakh crore against ₹1.60 lakh crore in the same month last year. That is growth of 10% (0.16 / 1.60). If refunds of ₹20,000 crore are paid, net collections are ₹1.56 lakh crore.
formula: Net GST collections = Gross GST collections - Refunds; Gross GST collections = CGST + SGST + IGST + Cess

short: An electronic document, generated online under GST rules, that must accompany goods above a set value while they are being transported.
kid: Before a toy truck carries sweets to another house, it gets a little note saying what is inside and where it is going. If someone stops the truck, the note shows everything is fair.
detail: An e-way bill is generated on the government's E-way Bill portal before goods are moved, under Rule 138 of the CGST Rules, rolled out from April 2018. Under the rules as of 2025, it is generally needed when a consignment is worth more than ₹50,000, though some states set different limits for movement within the state. Part A records the GST numbers of supplier and recipient, the invoice, the value and the product codes; Part B records the vehicle or transport document. Validity depends on distance, typically one day for every 200 km for ordinary cargo. The system curbs evasion by linking physical movement of goods to invoices. For markets, monthly e-way bill generation is a high-frequency indicator of trade and freight activity that often runs ahead of GST collections. A common confusion: an e-way bill is not a tax or an invoice; it is a movement document.
example: Say ABC Ltd ships machine parts worth ₹3 lakh by truck over 600 km. Because the value is above ₹50,000, it generates an e-way bill, and at one day per 200 km the bill is valid for 3 days. If e-way bills generated nationally rise from 10 crore in a month last year to 11 crore this month, that is 10% growth.
formula: Validity in days = Distance in km / 200, rounded up (ordinary cargo)

short: The Indian government's main policy think tank, chaired by the Prime Minister, which replaced the Planning Commission in 2015.
kid: It is like a group of clever helpers who sit with the head of the family and suggest good plans for the house. They give ideas, but they do not hand out the pocket money.
detail: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) was set up on 1 January 2015 by a Cabinet resolution, replacing the Planning Commission that had run India's Five-Year Plans since 1951. The Prime Minister is its chairperson, a full-time Vice Chairperson runs it, and its Governing Council includes all Chief Ministers. Unlike the Planning Commission, it has no power to allocate funds to ministries or states. It is an advisory think tank that drafts strategies, evaluates schemes and publishes state rankings such as the SDG India Index and indices on exports, innovation and fiscal health. For investors, its reports often signal policy direction, for example on asset monetisation, electric mobility or manufacturing. A common confusion is to think NITI Aayog decides how central taxes are shared with states: that is the job of the Finance Commission, a separate constitutional body.
example: The First Five-Year Plan began in 1951 and the Twelfth ended on 31 March 2017, so India ran 12 plans over 66 years, with annual plans filling some gaps. NITI Aayog, set up in January 2015, did not launch a 13th plan; it replaced Five-Year Plans with longer-term vision and strategy documents.

short: India's top constitutional auditor, who checks how the Centre, the states and government companies spend public money and reports to legislatures.
kid: When a class collects coins for a picnic, one careful child counts what was spent and tells everyone if anything went missing. That child does not spend the coins, only checks them.
detail: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is created by Article 148 of the Constitution, appointed by the President for six years or until age 65, and removable only like a Supreme Court judge. The CAG audits the receipts and spending of the Union and state governments and of bodies they substantially fund, and appoints the statutory auditors of government companies, including listed PSUs. Its reports go to the President or the Governor, are laid before Parliament or the state legislature, and are examined by the Public Accounts Committee. Reports can move markets and politics: the 2010 report on 2G spectrum put the presumptive loss at ₹1.76 lakh crore, and the 2012 coal block report estimated windfall gains to allottees of ₹1.86 lakh crore. A common confusion is to read such figures as cash actually lost; they are notional estimates, and the CAG audits but does not prosecute.
example: Say a state department was given ₹500 crore for rural roads and spent ₹420 crore, but the CAG finds that ₹35 crore went to projects never completed. Its report would flag ₹80 crore as unspent and ₹35 crore as wasteful spending, and the Public Accounts Committee would then question the department.

short: A constitutional body set up every five years to recommend how central tax revenue is shared between the Centre and the states, and among states.
kid: When a big family brings home fruit, a fair grandparent decides how much stays in the kitchen and how much goes to each child's room. Every few years the grandparent checks again to keep it fair.
detail: The Finance Commission is constituted by the President under Article 280 of the Constitution, normally every five years. Its main job is to recommend the vertical split, the share of the divisible pool of central taxes that goes to states, and the horizontal split, how that share is divided among states using criteria such as population, area, forest cover, income distance and demographic performance. It also recommends grants for revenue deficits, local bodies and disaster relief. The 14th Commission set the states' share at 42% for 2015-20, and the 15th, chaired by N.K. Singh, set it at 41% for 2021-26 after Jammu and Kashmir became a union territory. The 16th, chaired by Arvind Panagariya, covers 2026-27 to 2030-31. A common confusion is with NITI Aayog: the Finance Commission is a constitutional body setting formula-based transfers, while NITI Aayog only advises.
example: Under the 15th Finance Commission's 41% share, if the divisible pool in a year is ₹30 lakh crore, states together receive ₹12.3 lakh crore. A state with a 4% horizontal share would then get ₹49,200 crore.
formula: States' total share = Divisible pool x Vertical share (41% under the 15th Finance Commission)

short: The transfer of a fixed share of the Centre's tax collections to state governments, as recommended by the Finance Commission.
kid: When a family picks a basket of mangoes from the big tree, a fair part of the basket is handed to each child's home. Every home gets its part, so everyone can eat.
detail: Tax devolution is the constitutional sharing of central taxes with states under Article 270. The Centre collects taxes such as income tax, corporation tax and CGST, and a share of the divisible pool goes to states. The divisible pool is gross tax revenue minus cesses, surcharges and the cost of collection, which is why the Centre's growing reliance on cesses and surcharges is a sore point with states. The Finance Commission sets the states' share, 41% under the 15th Commission for 2021-26, and the formula that divides it among them. Devolved money is untied: states can spend it as they choose, unlike grants for specific schemes. It matters for investors because it shapes state finances, state borrowing through state development loans and capital spending. A common confusion is to apply the share to gross tax revenue rather than the divisible pool.
example: Suppose the Centre's gross tax revenue is ₹40 lakh crore, of which ₹4.5 lakh crore is cesses and surcharges and ₹0.5 lakh crore is the cost of collection. The divisible pool is ₹35 lakh crore, so at a 41% share the states receive ₹14.35 lakh crore. A state with a 4% horizontal share would get ₹57,400 crore.
formula: Divisible pool = Gross tax revenue - Cesses and surcharges - Cost of collection; Devolution to a state = Divisible pool x States' share x That state's horizontal share

short: The central government's yearly financial plan, presented to Parliament, setting out expected income, planned spending and tax changes for the coming year.
kid: Before the month starts, a family writes down how much pocket money will come in and what it will be spent on: food, school and toys. The country does the same thing once a year, for everyone.
detail: The Union Budget is the Annual Financial Statement that Article 112 requires the government to place before Parliament for each financial year, April to March. Since 2017 it has been presented on 1 February instead of the end of February, so that spending can begin on 1 April, and the railway budget was merged into it the same year. It sets out receipts and expenditure, the fiscal deficit target and borrowing plan, and announces tax changes through the Finance Bill. Markets watch it for borrowing, which moves bond yields, capital expenditure and sector-specific tax changes. In an election year the outgoing government usually presents an Interim Budget and seeks a vote on account under Article 116, permission to spend for a few months until a new government passes a full budget. A common confusion: the budget is a plan built on estimates, not audited actual figures.
example: Suppose a budget plans total spending of ₹50 lakh crore against receipts, excluding borrowing, of ₹34.5 lakh crore. The gap of ₹15.5 lakh crore is the fiscal deficit, which the government must borrow. If nominal GDP is expected at ₹350 lakh crore, the deficit is about 4.4% of GDP.
formula: Fiscal deficit = Total expenditure - (Revenue receipts + Non-debt capital receipts)

short: The Finance Ministry's yearly review of India's economy, written under the Chief Economic Adviser and tabled in Parliament just before the Union Budget.
kid: At the end of the school year, the teacher writes a report card for the whole class: what went well, what was hard and what to try next year. This is that report card for the country.
detail: The Economic Survey is prepared by the Economic Division of the Department of Economic Affairs under the Chief Economic Adviser, and is usually tabled in Parliament a day before the Union Budget. It reviews the past year across growth, inflation, public finances, trade, banking, agriculture, industry, services and jobs, and gives a growth projection for the coming year, often as a range. Many editions also argue for policy ideas in essay-style chapters. Economists and markets read it for the government's own view of growth and risks and for hints of reform. A common confusion is to treat it as a policy document: the Survey has no legal force and makes no tax or spending decisions, which come in the Budget and the Finance Bill. Note also that the Chief Economic Adviser is a Finance Ministry official, distinct from the RBI Governor and the Prime Minister's Economic Advisory Council.
example: Suppose the Survey projects real GDP growth of 6.3% to 6.8% for next year on a base of ₹190 lakh crore of real GDP. The range implies next year's real GDP of between ₹201.97 lakh crore and ₹202.92 lakh crore, a gap of ₹0.95 lakh crore between the low and high cases.

short: The government's projected receipts and spending for a year; revised estimates update them mid-year and actuals are the final recorded figures.
kid: At the start of a trip you guess you will spend ten coins on snacks. Halfway you change your guess to twelve, and at home you count what you really spent.
detail: Every Union Budget shows three kinds of figures. Budget estimates (BE) are projections for the coming financial year. Revised estimates (RE) update the current year's numbers about ten months in, based on actual trends, so the Budget presented on 1 February 2025 showed RE for 2024-25 alongside BE for 2025-26. Actuals are the final accounted figures, first shown in the Budget presented about ten months after the year ends, so the 2025-26 Budget carried actuals for 2023-24, though the Controller General of Accounts publishes monthly provisional data. Analysts compare BE with RE to see whether tax collections fell short, whether spending, especially capital expenditure, was cut, and whether the fiscal deficit target was met. A common confusion is to compare next year's BE with this year's BE: growth is better measured against the latest RE or actuals, because the starting point may already have been revised.
example: Suppose the government budgets capital expenditure of ₹11 lakh crore (BE), revises it to ₹10.2 lakh crore (RE) and finally spends ₹10 lakh crore (actuals). The shortfall against BE is ₹1 lakh crore, or about 9.1%. If next year's BE is ₹11.2 lakh crore, growth looks like 1.8% over the old BE but 9.8% over the RE.
formula: Shortfall = Budget estimate - Revised estimate (or Actual)

short: The Indian government's main account, into which nearly all its revenue and borrowing flows, and from which money can be spent only with Parliament's approval.
kid: A family keeps one big locked box for all the money that comes in. Nobody can take coins out unless the whole family agrees, except from a small tin kept for surprises.
detail: Under Article 266(1) of the Constitution, all revenues the Union government receives, all loans it raises and all loan repayments it receives go into the Consolidated Fund of India, and nothing can be withdrawn without a law passed by Parliament, usually the Appropriation Act. Some items, such as interest payments and the salaries of the President and Supreme Court judges, are charged on the Fund and not put to vote. The Contingency Fund of India under Article 267 is an advance account at the President's disposal for urgent, unforeseen spending, recouped once Parliament approves. The Public Account under Article 266(2) holds money the government handles as a banker or trustee, such as provident funds and small savings deposits, and needs no vote to spend. A common confusion is to treat Public Account money as government income; most of it belongs to savers. Each state has its own equivalent funds.
example: Say a flood needs ₹2,000 crore of emergency relief before Parliament meets. The government draws it from the Contingency Fund of India, whose corpus was raised from ₹500 crore to ₹30,000 crore in 2021, leaving ₹28,000 crore. Parliament later approves a supplementary grant and the ₹2,000 crore is put back from the Consolidated Fund.

short: The bill presented with the Union Budget that puts its tax proposals into law; once Parliament passes it, it becomes the Finance Act.
kid: The family writes a list of new house rules about who pays for what. Once everyone signs the list, the rules really start.
detail: The Finance Bill carries the tax changes announced in the Union Budget, such as new income tax slabs, customs duty changes or amendments to capital gains rules, and is introduced in the Lok Sabha right after the budget speech. It is usually certified as a Money Bill under Article 110, so the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject. Under the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 1931, certain declared provisions take effect immediately but lapse after 75 days unless enacted, which is why the Bill is usually passed by March. A separate Appropriation Bill, under Article 114, authorises withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund for spending. A common confusion is to think the budget speech changes the law by itself: tax rates change only through the Finance Act or the provisional-collection rules, and amendments during passage can alter what was announced.
example: In the July 2024 Budget, the Finance Bill raised the tax on listed long-term capital gains from 10% to 12.5% with effect from budget day. On ₹5 lakh of taxable long-term gains booked after that date, tax before surcharge and cess rose from ₹50,000 to ₹62,500, an extra ₹12,500.

short: India's way of grouping large numbers in lakhs and crores: one lakh is 100,000 and one crore is 10 million.
kid: If you put a hundred thousand marbles in one giant bag, people in India call that bag a lakh. A hundred of those giant bags together make a crore.
detail: The Indian numbering system groups digits differently from the international system. After the first three digits from the right, commas come every two digits: one lakh is written 1,00,000 (100,000) and one crore is 1,00,00,000 (10 million). Larger amounts are built by stacking units, so a lakh crore is 1,00,00,00,00,000, or one trillion. Company results, budgets and Indian news use these units throughout: market capitalisation in crore, government spending in lakh crore. Lakh is sometimes written L or Lac, and crore Cr. The common confusion comes when converting to millions and billions: 10 lakh is one million, 100 crore is one billion and 1 lakh crore is one trillion, so ₹500 crore is ₹5 billion, not ₹500 million. Older units such as arab (100 crore) are rarely used in financial writing today.
example: Say ABC Ltd reports revenue of ₹2,500 crore. That is 2,500 x 1,00,00,000 = ₹25,000,000,000, or ₹25 billion in international terms. A government programme costing ₹1.5 lakh crore equals ₹1,50,000 crore, or ₹1.5 trillion.
formula: 1 lakh = 100,000; 1 crore = 100 lakh = 10 million; 1 lakh crore = 1 trillion

short: A government scheme that pays manufacturers cash incentives linked to how much extra they produce and sell in India above a base year.
kid: A teacher says: for every extra drawing you make this week beyond last week, you get a sticker. So everyone tries to make more drawings.
detail: Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes, launched in 2020 starting with mobile phones and electronic components, pay eligible companies a percentage of their incremental sales of goods made in India over a base year, usually for about five years. They were extended to 14 sectors, including pharmaceuticals, automobiles and components, specialty steel, textiles, food processing, solar modules, white goods and advanced chemistry cell batteries, with a combined outlay of about ₹1.97 lakh crore. Companies must commit minimum investment and meet yearly sales thresholds to qualify. The aim is to build scale, attract global supply chains and boost exports. For investors, PLI approvals and payouts can lift a company's margins and capacity plans, but the incentive is temporary and often tapers, so analysts check whether the business stays profitable without it. A common confusion: most PLI schemes pay on incremental sales, not on investment or total sales.
example: Say ABC Electronics Ltd had base-year sales of ₹1,000 crore and sells ₹1,600 crore of eligible India-made goods this year. Incremental sales are ₹600 crore, so at a hypothetical incentive rate of 5% it receives ₹30 crore. If its profit before the incentive is ₹48 crore, the incentive alone adds 62.5% to profit.
formula: PLI incentive = Incentive rate x (Eligible sales this year - Base-year sales)

short: A government campaign, launched in 2014, to make India a global manufacturing hub by attracting investment and easing rules for factories.
kid: Instead of always buying toys from a faraway shop, the town builds its own toy workshop. Then children can buy toys made by their neighbours, and the neighbours get work too.
detail: Make in India was launched on 25 September 2014 to raise manufacturing's share of the economy and create jobs, initially focusing on 25 sectors. It combined easier foreign investment rules, faster approvals, investor facilitation and ease-of-doing-business reforms. Atmanirbhar Bharat, or self-reliant India, announced in May 2020 with a stimulus package of about ₹20 lakh crore, extended the idea toward reducing import dependence in strategic areas, using tools such as PLI schemes, higher customs duties on some goods and preference for local suppliers in government purchases. These policies shape which sectors attract capital. A common confusion is to read self-reliance as closing the economy: the stated aim is to build domestic capacity and plug into global supply chains, though critics point to rising tariffs. Progress is often judged against the old goal of a 25% manufacturing share of GDP, which, as of 2025, has stayed in the mid-teens.
example: Suppose manufacturing output is ₹45 lakh crore in a ₹300 lakh crore economy, a 15% share. Reaching a 25% share with the economy unchanged would need manufacturing output of ₹75 lakh crore, or ₹30 lakh crore more.

short: A monthly index measuring how much India's factories, mines and power plants produce compared with a base year.
kid: Every month someone counts how many toys, bricks and buckets of coal the town's workshops made. If the number goes up, the workshops were busier than before.
detail: The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) is compiled by the National Statistics Office under MoSPI and released monthly with a lag of roughly four to six weeks. It tracks the volume of output in manufacturing, which carries roughly three-quarters of the weight, mining and electricity. It is also shown by use: primary goods, capital goods, intermediate goods, infrastructure and construction goods, consumer durables and consumer non-durables. The headline number in the news is year-on-year growth in the index, not the index level. Investors use it to gauge the industrial cycle: capital goods growth hints at investment and consumer durables at urban demand. Common confusions: IIP covers only industry, not services or agriculture, so it is not GDP growth; a weak month last year can inflate growth through a low base; and early numbers are revised later. The base year and weights are updated periodically.
example: Suppose the IIP stands at 152.0 in a month against 145.0 in the same month a year earlier. Industrial output growth is (152.0 / 145.0 - 1) x 100 = about 4.8%.
formula: IIP growth (%) = (Index this month / Index same month last year - 1) x 100

short: A monthly index tracking output of eight basic industries: coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement and electricity.
kid: Before you can make toys, you need wood, paint, glue and lights in the workshop. This counts how much of those basic things the country made each month.
detail: The Index of Eight Core Industries (ICI) is released monthly by the Office of the Economic Adviser in the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, ahead of the IIP for the same month. The eight industries are coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement and electricity, with refinery products, electricity and steel carrying the largest weights. Together they make up about 40% of the weight of items in the IIP, so core sector growth is treated as an early signal of industrial output. They also supply inputs to construction, transport and manufacturing, so weakness here often spreads. A common confusion is to treat core sector growth as total industrial growth: the index leaves out most manufacturing, such as cars, phones and consumer goods, so the two can diverge, and its numbers are revised after the first release.
example: Suppose the core index is 160.0 this month against 152.0 a year ago, so core sector growth is (160.0 / 152.0 - 1) x 100 = about 5.3%. Because the eight industries carry roughly 40% of IIP weight, a rough guide to their direct contribution to IIP growth is 0.40 x 5.3 = about 2.1 percentage points.
formula: Core sector growth (%) = (Index this month / Index same month last year - 1) x 100

short: An index tracking the prices of goods at the wholesale, bulk-trading stage in India, used to measure wholesale inflation.
kid: Before sweets reach the corner shop, the shopkeeper buys big boxes from a big seller. This checks whether those big boxes cost more this year than last year.
detail: The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) is compiled monthly by the Office of the Economic Adviser in the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade. It covers goods only, in three groups: primary articles such as food and minerals, fuel and power, and manufactured products, which carry about two-thirds of the weight. WPI inflation is the year-on-year change in the index. Because it captures prices at the producer and bulk-trade stage, it helps track companies' raw-material costs, is used in contracts with price-variation clauses and serves as a deflator in national accounts. The common confusion is with CPI inflation: CPI measures retail prices households pay, including services such as rent, education and health, and the RBI's inflation target is set in CPI terms, not WPI. The two can diverge sharply when global commodity prices swing, since WPI gives heavier weight to fuel and metals.
example: Suppose the WPI is 156.0 this month and was 153.0 in the same month last year. WPI inflation is (156.0 / 153.0 - 1) x 100 = about 1.96%, or 2.0% rounded. If CPI inflation in the same month is 4.0%, retail prices are rising about twice as fast as wholesale prices.
formula: WPI inflation (%) = (WPI this month / WPI same month last year - 1) x 100

aliases: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
hl: ministry of statistics and programme implementation
short: India's Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, whose National Statistics Office publishes GDP, retail inflation, industrial output and employment data.
kid: It is like the school helper who counts everything: how many children came, how many books were read, how many lunches were eaten. Everyone else uses those counts to make good choices.
detail: The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) is the central government's official statistics ministry. Its National Statistics Office (NSO), formed in 2019 by merging the Central Statistics Office (CSO) and the National Sample Survey Office, compiles national accounts, including quarterly GDP and advance estimates, the Consumer Price Index used for the RBI's inflation target, the Index of Industrial Production, and surveys such as the Periodic Labour Force Survey and household consumption surveys. Markets move on its release days because these numbers feed RBI policy, demand forecasts and bond yields, and it publishes a release calendar in advance. A common confusion is to credit MoSPI with every indicator: WPI and the core sector index come from the Commerce Ministry's DPIIT, and GST data from the Finance Ministry. Periodic base-year revisions to GDP, CPI and IIP can reshape historical series.
example: Suppose quarterly real GDP comes in at ₹47.0 lakh crore against ₹44.0 lakh crore in the same quarter a year earlier. The NSO would report real growth of (47.0 / 44.0 - 1) x 100 = about 6.8%.

short: Early official estimates of India's GDP for a financial year, released before the year ends and later replaced by provisional and revised estimates.
kid: Before a race is over, the coach guesses your finishing time from how you are running so far. After the race, the coach checks the clock and fixes the guess.
detail: India's GDP for a financial year is estimated in stages by the National Statistics Office. Traditionally, the first advance estimates come in early January, using data for roughly the first seven or eight months, so they can feed into the Union Budget; the second advance estimates follow at the end of February with third-quarter data; provisional estimates arrive at the end of May with fourth-quarter data; and first, second and third revised estimates follow in the next three Februaries as fuller data, such as company filings and annual surveys, come in. Markets react to each release because growth surprises change earnings expectations, RBI policy and fiscal maths, since the deficit target is a share of nominal GDP. A common confusion is to treat the first number as final: revisions of half a percentage point or more are common, and base-year changes can reshape the whole series.
example: Say the first advance estimate puts real GDP growth at 6.4%, the provisional estimate at 6.5% and the first revised estimate at 7.1%. The total upward revision is 0.7 percentage points. On the previous year's real GDP of ₹180 lakh crore, that 0.7-point difference is worth ₹1.26 lakh crore of output.

short: India's official household survey of jobs, measuring how many people work, look for work or are unemployed, run by the National Statistics Office.
kid: Someone visits many homes and asks: who has a job, who is looking for one, and who is at school or at home? Adding up the answers shows how many grown-ups have work.
detail: The Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), launched in 2017 by the National Sample Survey Office, now part of the National Statistics Office, is India's main source of official employment data. It reports three key ratios: the labour force participation rate (LFPR), the share of the population working or seeking work; the worker population ratio; and the unemployment rate, the share of the labour force without work. Results are given by usual status, based on the past year, and current weekly status, based on the past week. Since 2025 it also publishes monthly estimates and quarterly estimates covering rural as well as urban India, alongside annual reports. Economists and investors use it to judge consumption strength and the quality of growth. A common confusion is that a low unemployment rate means plentiful good jobs: many Indians are self-employed or in unpaid family work, so participation and job quality matter as much.
example: Suppose a district has 10 lakh people aged 15 and above, of whom 5.5 lakh are working and 0.3 lakh are looking for work. The labour force is 5.8 lakh, so the LFPR is 58% and the unemployment rate is 0.3 / 5.8 = about 5.2%.
formula: LFPR = Labour force / Population x 100; Unemployment rate = Unemployed / Labour force x 100

short: Micro, small and medium enterprises: smaller businesses classified in India by their investment in plant and machinery and their annual turnover.
kid: Think of the corner bakery, the tailor down the road and the little workshop that makes buckets. These small shops and workshops together give lots of people work.
detail: In India, micro, small and medium enterprises are defined under the MSMED Act, 2006, using combined limits on investment in plant and machinery and annual turnover. Under the rules as of 2025, revised from April 2025, a micro unit has investment up to ₹2.5 crore and turnover up to ₹10 crore, a small unit up to ₹25 crore and ₹100 crore, and a medium unit up to ₹125 crore and ₹500 crore. Firms register free online through Udyam registration to access priority-sector lending, credit guarantees and procurement preferences. MSMEs provide a large share of output, exports and jobs, so their health feeds consumption and bank asset quality. Under tax rules as of 2025, buyers can deduct dues to micro and small suppliers in the purchase year only if paid within 15 days, or 45 if agreed. A common confusion: MSME is a legal category, not any small listed company.
example: Say a manufacturer has ₹20 crore invested in plant and machinery and turnover of ₹80 crore. Under the 2025 limits, both figures are within the small-enterprise caps of ₹25 crore and ₹100 crore, so it is a small enterprise. If its turnover grows to ₹120 crore, it crosses the small cap and is classified as medium.

short: The part of the economy made up of small unregistered businesses and workers without written contracts, social security or regular tax records.
kid: Think of the person selling fruit from a cart or fixing shoes on the pavement. They work hard every day, but there is no big office, no paper contract and no one writing it all down.
detail: The informal or unorganised sector covers unincorporated enterprises, usually proprietorships and partnerships with few workers, that are not registered as companies and often keep no formal accounts: street vendors, small shops, home-based workers, small farms and construction labour. In India it employs a large majority of workers and contributes a substantial share of output, which official statistics capture partly through surveys such as the NSO's Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises. It matters for markets because shocks such as demonetisation in 2016, the GST rollout in 2017 and the 2020 lockdowns hit informal firms hardest, while formalisation can shift market share to listed companies with organised supply chains. A common confusion is between the informal sector and informal employment: a large registered company can still hire contract workers without social security, and those jobs count as informal employment even though the employer is formal.
example: Suppose a town has 1,000 workers: 180 have formal jobs with provident fund and paid leave, and 820 work in small shops, farms or as casual labour. Informal employment is 820 / 1,000 = 82% of the workforce. If 50 of the casual workers join a new factory with social security, the informal share falls to 77%.
formula: Informal employment share = Informal workers / Total workers x 100

short: A company in which the central or a state government owns a majority stake, usually 51% or more, such as ONGC, NTPC or Coal India.
kid: Imagine a lemonade stand owned mostly by the whole town instead of one family. The town picks who runs it, and some of the coins it makes go back to the town.
detail: A public sector undertaking is a company or corporation majority-owned by government. Under the Companies Act, 2013, a government company is one in which the Centre and/or states hold at least 51% of paid-up share capital. Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) are those owned by the Centre and overseen by the Department of Public Enterprises; many, such as ONGC, NTPC, Coal India and BHEL, are listed with the government holding more than half. Public sector banks such as SBI are government-controlled too but are governed by banking laws and usually counted separately from CPSEs. For investors, PSU stocks often pay high dividends because the government relies on them for revenue, and they tend to trade at lower valuations because of policy risk, such as being asked to absorb fuel price increases. A common confusion: 'PSU' in a name like 'banking and PSU debt fund' refers to their bonds, not shares.
example: Say the government owns 70% of ABC Ltd, a hypothetical listed PSU, and the company declares a total dividend of ₹2,000 crore. The government receives ₹1,400 crore and other shareholders share the remaining ₹600 crore.

short: Status tiers given to large, profitable central public sector enterprises, letting their boards invest and form ventures with less government approval.
kid: When a big child shows they are careful and responsible, the parents let them buy things on their own without asking every time. The most trusted children get the most freedom.
detail: The Ratna scheme of the Department of Public Enterprises gives financial and operational freedom to strong central public sector enterprises in three tiers. Miniratnas must be consistently profitable with positive net worth. Navratnas are drawn from Category I Miniratnas with strong performance scores, and their boards can invest up to the lower of ₹1,000 crore or 15% of net worth in a single project without government approval. Maharatnas, a tier created in 2009-10, must already be Navratnas, be listed, and show three-year averages above ₹25,000 crore of turnover, ₹15,000 crore of net worth and ₹5,000 crore of net profit, with a significant global presence; their boards can invest up to 15% of net worth, capped at ₹5,000 crore, in one project. ONGC, NTPC, Coal India and SAIL are Maharatnas. These limits follow DPE guidelines as of 2025 and can change. A common confusion: Ratna status signals autonomy, not creditworthiness.
example: Say ABC Ltd, a hypothetical CPSE, has averaged ₹40,000 crore of turnover, ₹18,000 crore of net worth and ₹4,500 crore of net profit over three years. It clears the turnover and net-worth tests for Maharatna but misses the ₹5,000 crore profit test by ₹500 crore, so it stays a Navratna. Its board can approve a single project of up to ₹1,000 crore on its own, since that is lower than 15% of its net worth, ₹2,700 crore.

short: The government selling part or all of its shareholding in public sector companies, to raise money or to hand control to private owners.
kid: The town owns a big part of the lemonade stand. It lets other families buy some of that part to pay for a new playground, and sometimes it hands the whole stand to a family who will run it.
detail: Disinvestment is the sale of government equity in public sector enterprises, handled for the Centre by DIPAM. Minority sales, through IPOs, offers for sale on stock exchanges, ETFs such as the CPSE ETF or buybacks, raise cash while the government keeps control. Strategic disinvestment, or privatisation, sells a controlling stake and management to a buyer, as with Air India, sold to Tata Sons in a deal completed in January 2022. Proceeds count as non-debt capital receipts in the Union Budget, so they narrow the fiscal deficit and reduce borrowing. For markets, large offers add share supply and can weigh on a PSU's price in the short run, while privatisation can re-rate a company if investors expect better management. A common confusion is with asset monetisation, where only the right to use an asset is leased and ownership stays with the government. Annual targets are often missed.
example: Say the government owns 75% of ABC Ltd, a hypothetical PSU with 100 crore shares. Selling 10 crore shares through an offer for sale at ₹150 each raises ₹1,500 crore and cuts its stake to 65%, so it keeps control. Selling a further 16 crore shares would take its stake to 49% and end its majority.
formula: Disinvestment proceeds = Shares sold x Sale price per share

aliases: Department of Investment and Public Asset Management
hl: department of investment and public asset management
short: The Finance Ministry department that manages the central government's shareholdings in public sector companies, including stake sales, dividends and asset monetisation.
kid: Think of one grown-up in the family who looks after the family's parts of different shops in town. They decide when to swap a part for coins, and make sure each shop sends home the family's fair bit.
detail: The Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) sits within the Ministry of Finance. It began as the Department of Disinvestment in 1999 and was renamed in April 2016, when its mandate widened from selling stakes to managing government equity as an investment. It runs minority stake sales through offers for sale, IPOs and ETFs, handles strategic disinvestments, and issues guidelines to CPSEs on capital management, such as minimum dividend payouts, bonus issues and buybacks. It also supports the monetisation of non-core assets and land of CPSEs. Markets follow DIPAM because its announcements signal upcoming share supply in PSU stocks, dividend expectations and privatisation plans. A common confusion: DIPAM manages the government's ownership, while oversight of CPSEs as enterprises sits with the Department of Public Enterprises, and the National Monetisation Pipeline for infrastructure was prepared by NITI Aayog with line ministries.
example: Say DIPAM runs an offer for sale of 5 crore shares of ABC Ltd, a hypothetical listed PSU, at a floor price of ₹200 when the stock last closed at ₹215. The floor is a discount of about 7%, and if the offer is fully sold at the floor it raises ₹1,000 crore.

short: A government plan to lease out operating public infrastructure, such as roads and power lines, to private investors for upfront cash while keeping ownership.
kid: The town lets a family run its finished swimming pool for some years and keep the entry tickets. The family pays the town now, the town builds a new park with it, and later the pool comes back to the town.
detail: The National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP), announced in August 2021 and prepared by NITI Aayog with infrastructure ministries, listed operating central government assets worth an estimated ₹6 lakh crore to be monetised from 2021-22 to 2024-25. Roads, railways and power transmission made up the biggest shares, alongside gas pipelines, telecom, warehousing, ports, airports and stadiums. Assets are monetised through models such as toll-operate-transfer concessions, operations and maintenance leases, and Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs). The government receives upfront payments or a revenue share, recycles the money into new projects, and gets the asset back at the end of the term. The 2025-26 Budget announced a second Asset Monetisation Plan for 2025-30 aiming at ₹10 lakh crore. For investors, the NMP feeds the supply of InvITs and road and power concessions. A common confusion is to equate monetisation with privatisation: ownership of the underlying asset is not sold.
example: Suppose the government leases a highway stretch earning about ₹150 crore a year in tolls to a private operator for 20 years under a toll-operate-transfer contract, receiving ₹1,800 crore upfront. If tolls stay flat, the operator expects ₹3,000 crore of toll collections over the term (₹150 crore x 20) before costs, while the government spends the ₹1,800 crore on new roads and takes the highway back after 20 years.
